title: Study design and methods
text:
Provisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This page explains, in plain language and without code, what the maps show and why they are drawn this way. The general background is on Methodological background. The formal specification is the analysis plan. Three kinds of note mark where the description stands:

title: Study design and methods
text:
What is mapped
Each study’s paper computed a few summaries for every UNOS region: how many transplants used a donor type or technology, and what percentage that was. The maps show those summaries as published; nothing new is estimated. Every state in a region is shaded with the region’s value.
Specified in: §2 Objectives, §6 Estimation.

Decision pending: what each percentage is a share of, and so how its legend should read (D3 in SETUP-NOTES.md).

title: Study design and methods
text:
Where the geography comes from
The region assignment of each state and the region outlines come from sRtr, built from the same Census boundaries and region table the original maps used. Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico are left out, as in the original maps.
Specified in: §4 Data sources, §5 Study populations and unit definitions.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Which transplant centers are shown
Adult heart-transplant centers, from HRSA’s transplant-center layer, at their true locations. Pediatric centers are left out by the original maps’ rule: centers whose name contains “Children”, except two that also transplant adults.
Specified in: §5.

Decision pending: whether to use today’s HRSA layer, a dated snapshot for each study, or the original file (D1), and whether the name rule still identifies pediatric centers in the HRSA layer (D2), both in SETUP-NOTES.md.

title: Study design and methods
text:
How the maps are drawn
Every layer is projected to NAD83 / Conus Albers, and each map is drawn twice: with ggplot2, matching the published maps’ look, and with tmap, adding an inset that enlarges the Northeast.
Specified in: §2, §7 Linkage and geography.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Publication of the regional values
The regional values are published in each paper, so the spreadsheets and the maps drawn from them are public and kept in the repository.
Specified in: §12 Disclosure control.
Project documentsRepository blueprint Code

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

title: 1. Map geography
text:
Provisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This script builds the map layers every study shares: states with their UNOS region, region outlines, region numbers, adult heart-transplant centers and the extent of the Northeast inset.

title: 1. Map geography
text:
States and regions
In the original scripts this took three files: a spreadsheet listing each region’s states, the 2018 Census state shapefile, and code to split, pivot and join them. sRtr was built from exactly that code, so the result now ships with the package as UNOS_regions_sf: one row per state (the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia) with its region. get_hrsa_optn_regions() dissolves the states into one outline per region. Both are put in map_crs, so every layer shares one projection.


Click to show/hide R Code
# State polygons tagged with UNOS region, built into sRtr. These replace the
# Census shapefile and the hand-split region table in the original code.
region_states <- UNOS_regions_sf |>
  st_transform(map_crs)

# One outline per region, replacing the original st_union() step
region_outlines <- get_hrsa_optn_regions() |>
  st_transform(map_crs)

title: 1. Map geography
text:
Region numbers
st_point_on_surface() returns a point guaranteed to fall inside each region. A centroid can fall outside a region whose shape is irregular. These points replace the hand-entered label positions the original maps read from a spreadsheet.


Click to show/hide R Code
# A point inside each region for its number, replacing the hand-entered
# label positions in "UNOS region labels.xlsx"
region_labels <- region_outlines |>
  st_point_on_surface() |>
  mutate(label = str_remove(Region, "Region "))

title: 1. Map geography
text:
Transplant centers
The original maps used a copy of an HRSA transplant-center file downloaded once. get_hrsa_transplant_centers() downloads the current layer from HRSA each time it runs (Health Resources and Services Administration, n.d.), which is then narrowed to adult heart centers (see Functions).

Decision pending: the current layer shows centers as they are today, not as they were during each study period. Whether to use it, a dated snapshot for each study, or the original file is decision D1 in SETUP-NOTES.md.



Click to show/hide R Code
# Current HRSA transplant-center layer, filtered to adult heart centers
heart_centers <- get_hrsa_transplant_centers() |>
  select_adult_centers(
    organ = center_organ,
    adult_exceptions = adult_center_exceptions,
    crs = map_crs
  )

title: 1. Map geography
text:
The Northeast inset
The inset shows the bounding box of Regions 1, 2 and 9, from Maine to West Virginia.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Extent of the Northeast regions, enlarged in the tmap inset
northeast_bbox <- region_outlines |>
  filter(Region %in% northeast_regions) |>
  st_bbox()

title: Original RMDs
text:
The R Markdown files that drew the published maps, kept in original/ as the provenance of each map. They are shown here for comparison and are never run. The only change from the files as written is that the folder paths on the author’s computer have been removed, leaving the file names.
All three map RMDs share one pipeline: split a spreadsheet’s “Region N: state, state, …” text into states, join the states to a Census shapefile, dissolve them into regions with st_union(), read a downloaded HRSA center file, and plot in longitude and latitude. The Map geography and Functions pages show what replaces each step.

Import and clean table of regions and shape files for states

#Import UNOS region data
UNOS_regions <- UNOS_regions <- 
  #Import Shivank's data from UNOS regions into R
  read_excel("UNOS regions.xlsx") %>%
  #Split column that contains Regions and which states they contain
  separate(Region, c("Region", "B"),sep=":") %>%
  #Split list of states into 7 separate variables
  separate(B, c("State1","State2","State3","State4", "State5", "State6", "State7"), ,sep=",") %>%
  #Trim leading spaces
  mutate_at(vars(contains("State")), str_trim) %>%
  #Change to long format and drop extraneous variable that results
   pivot_longer(
   cols = starts_with("State"),
   names_to = "StateNumber",
   values_to = "State",
   values_drop_na = TRUE) %>%
  select(-StateNumber) %>%
  #Convert percentage variable into percentage (it imports as a raw proportion)
  mutate(Percentage_HT_HCV=100*Percentage_HT_HCV) %>%
  mutate(Percentage_HT_total=100*Percentage_HT_total)
  

#Import State level data
us_states <- read_sf("cb_2018_us_state_20m/cb_2018_us_state_20m.shp") %>%
  select(NAME, geometry) %>%
  filter(!(NAME %in% c("Alaska", "Hawaii", "Puerto Rico"))) %>%
  rename(State=NAME)

#Import region labels
UNOS_region_labels <- read_excel("UNOS region labels.xlsx")

#Import transplant centers
Transplant_centers <- read_csv("Transplant centers.csv") %>%
  select(OTCName, OrganTransplantationCenterServiceTypeDescription, Latitude, Longitude) %>%
  filter(OrganTransplantationCenterServiceTypeDescription=="Heart")

#Looked into removing centers with "Children" in the name, but some may also have adults?
Transplant_centers<-Transplant_centers %>%filter(str_detect(Transplant_centers$OTCName,"Children")=="FALSE" | 
                               (OTCName %in% c("Memorial Regional Hospital/Joe DiMaggio Children's Hospital", 
                                                "Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center & Children's Hospital")))

#Merge files


MergedStates<-inner_join(UNOS_regions, us_states, by="State") %>%st_as_sf()

UNOS_region_map<-MergedStates%>%  
  group_by(Region) %>% 
  summarize(geometry = st_union(geometry))

ShivankMap20210214<-ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data=MergedStates,mapping=aes(fill = Percentage_HT_HCV), 
                                color="black", size = 0.25)+
  geom_sf(data=UNOS_region_map,color="black", fill=NA, size = 1)+
  theme_void()+
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "OrYel")


ggsave("ShivankMap20210214.png", 
       plot=ShivankMap20210214)

#Will add transplant centers to map
ggplot()+
    geom_sf(data=MergedStates,mapping=aes(fill = Percentage_HT_HCV), 
            color="#838383", size = 0.25)+
    geom_sf(data=UNOS_region_map,color="black", fill=NA, size = 1)+
    geom_jitter(data=Transplant_centers, mapping=aes(x=Longitude, y=Latitude), alpha=0.5, 
                height = 0.3, width = 0.3) +
    theme_void()+
    scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "OrYel")



MergedStates%>%ggplot()+geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill = Number_HT_HCV), 
                                color="white")+theme_void()+
  scale_fill_continuous_diverging(palette = "Purple-Green")

ggplot()+
    geom_sf(data=MergedStates,mapping=aes(fill = Percentage_HT_HCV), 
            color="black")+
    theme_void()+
    scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "OrYel") + 
  geom_richtext(data=UNOS_region_labels, fill = NA, color="blue", label.color = NA, 
                mapping=aes(x=Lon, y=Lat, label=Region, family="Comic Sans MS"))

The map, in ggplot2
This replaces the original maps’ geom_sf() calls with two changes. First, the plot is drawn in map_crs (coord_sf(crs = ...)) rather than in longitude and latitude, so the country is not stretched east to west. Second, centers are drawn with geom_sf() at their true locations; the original geom_jitter() moved each point randomly by up to 0.3 degrees, which is about 30 km. # Map one measure: states shaded by region value, region outlines on top,
# region numbers, and optionally transplant centers at their true locations.
map_regions_ggplot <- function(region_states, region_outlines, region_labels,
                               fill_var, legend_title, centers = NULL,
                               palette, na_fill, crs) {
  region_map <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(
      data = region_states,
      mapping = aes(fill = .data[[fill_var]]),
      colour = "grey55",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_sf(data = region_outlines, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_sf_text(
      data = region_labels,
      mapping = aes(label = label),
      colour = "navy",
      fontface = "bold",
      size = 3.5
    )

  if (!is.null(centers)) {
    region_map <- region_map +
      geom_sf(data = centers, size = 1.2, alpha = 0.6)
  }

  region_map +
    scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = palette, na.value = na_fill) +
    coord_sf(crs = crs, datum = NA) +
    labs(fill = legend_title) +
    theme_void()
}

text:
The map, in tmap, with a Northeast inset
The New England and Mid-Atlantic states are small and their transplant centers crowd together. tmap’s tm_inset() draws the same map again, enlarged to the extent of the Northeast regions, in a corner of the main map, and outlines that extent on the main map.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The same map in tmap, with the Northeast enlarged in an inset so its small
# states and crowded centers can be read.
map_regions_tmap <- function(region_states, region_outlines, region_labels,
                             fill_var, legend_title, centers = NULL,
                             inset_bbox, palette, na_fill) {
  region_map <- tm_shape(region_states) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = fill_var,
      fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(
        values = sequential_hcl(7, palette = palette),
        value.na = na_fill
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legend_title),
      col = "grey55",
      lwd = 0.5
    ) +
    tm_shape(region_outlines) +
    tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.5) +
    tm_shape(region_labels) +
    tm_text("label", col = "navy", fontface = "bold", size = 0.8)

  if (!is.null(centers)) {
    region_map <- region_map +
      tm_shape(centers) +
      tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill_alpha = 0.6)
  }

  region_map +
    tm_inset(inset_bbox, position = c("right", "bottom"), width = 14, height = 14) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
}

Each found that uptake varied widely across the eleven UNOS regions, and each showed that variation with a map. More on the clinical background page.

title: Overview
text:
What this site does
It reproduces each study’s regional map, and teaches how to draw it with the sRtr package. The original maps were built from a hand-split region table, a local Census shapefile, a hand-entered sheet of label positions and a downloaded list of transplant centers. sRtr holds the region geography and downloads the current HRSA transplant-center layer, so each map now takes a few package calls. Every layer is projected to NAD83 / Conus Albers before plotting, and each map is drawn twice: once with ggplot2, and once with tmap with the crowded Northeast enlarged in an inset.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Each study’s regional summary, one row per region, is joined to sRtr’s state polygons and shaded by region. Study design and methods explains each choice, and the authoritative specification is the analysis plan. The original code is on Original RMDs.

title: Overview

Status
In development. The code is in place for three studies; the maps themselves are added to the site once they have been drawn from the regional spreadsheets. The COVID-19 donor study (Madan et al. 2023) and the donor offer acceptance study (Ramineni et al. 2026) have no maps yet. Open decisions are listed in SETUP-NOTES.md until they are filed as issues.

title: Methodological background
text: General mapping ideas the code relies on, with nothing specific to one study.

title: Methodological background
text:
UNOS regions
The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network divides the United States into eleven regions, each a group of states. Several UNOS regions do not follow state lines exactly (for example, parts of a state can belong to a neighbouring region); sRtr assigns each state to a single region, so a state-level map is an approximation at those edges (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026).

title: Methodological background
text:
A region-level choropleth
When the value being mapped belongs to a region, every state in the region is shaded the same. Thin state lines under thick region outlines remind the reader of that: the shading says nothing about any state alone.

title: Methodological background
text:
Projections
Spatial data store positions in a coordinate reference system (CRS). Longitude and latitude are angles, not distances, and drawing them as if they were x and y stretches the United States east to west and makes northern states look larger than they are. An equal-area projection such as NAD83 / Conus Albers (EPSG:5070) keeps areas comparable across the country, which matters when shaded area is what the eye reads. The safest habit is to transform every layer to the one CRS with sf::st_transform() before plotting, as the HOPE-CDC analysis does, rather than relying on the plotting function to reconcile them.

title: Methodological background
text:
Points, not jitter
Jittering adds random noise to positions so that overlapping points separate. On a map it moves each place somewhere it is not. Drawing points at their true positions, partly transparent, and enlarging crowded areas in an inset shows overlap honestly.

title: Methodological background
text:
Insets
An inset repeats part of the map at a larger scale in a corner of the figure. In the Northeast, small states and many centers close together make the main map hard to read; an inset of Regions 1, 2 and 9 makes them legible without shrinking the rest of the country.

title: Methodological background
text:
What the result looks like



The ggplot2 version of a region map, drawn from synthetic values, not study results, with synthetic center locations. The Northeast is crowded, which is what the tmap inset addresses.

title: Clinical background
text:
Too few donor hearts are available for the patients who need them, and much recent work in heart transplantation has been about safely using donors and techniques that were once avoided. The studies mapped on this site each followed one of these through the UNOS registry.

HCV donors. Effective antiviral treatment made it possible to use organs from donors with hepatitis C. Between 2015 and 2020, the share of multiorgan heart transplants using HCV donors rose from none to 14%, with wide variation across regions and center volumes; one-year survival of heart-kidney recipients was similar with and without HCV donors (Madan et al. 2021).
DCD donors. Hearts from donors after circulatory death, rather than brain death, became a growing source of organs. Their use in multiorgan heart transplantation rose from 1% in early 2020 to 12% in early 2023, again with wide regional variation, and six-month survival after heart-kidney transplantation was similar to that with brain-death donors (Madan et al. 2024).
Ex vivo machine perfusion. Keeping a donor heart perfused during transport, rather than on ice, may protect hearts from older donors or travelling long distances. Its use in transplants from brain-death donors rose from about 1% in 2020 to about 11% in 2024, driven by a few high-volume centers, with survival comparable to cold storage (Madan et al. 2025).

In each study, a map showed at a glance where use was concentrated.

The project
This is a teaching repository. It reproduces the UNOS-region maps from a series of published heart-transplantation registry studies (HCV donors, DCD donors and ex vivo machine perfusion so far) and shows how to draw them with the sRtr package instead of hand-built region tables, local shapefiles and downloaded center lists. Cohort flow (not used here: this project draws no cohort) uses the flowchart package, so the STROBE flow diagram and the analytic cohort come from the same code. Every inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter(), in the plan’s order. Never remove people from the cohort outside the flowchart. Record-level processing (cleaning claims, choosing among a person’s records) is fine. An analysis that uses fewer people than the cohort (complete cases, a subgroup) reports its own number with that analysis. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final step (fc_view(what = "data")). Flowchart labels are built from constants in setup.R.
Code lists carry each code’s category, code system and version, and matching rule (exact or prefix). Check every code against the official code set. Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every interval join and every join of records to people, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows.
Dates and windows are written as inclusive offsets from the index date, matching the plan, and the edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.

This repository reproduces the regional maps from a series of published heart-transplantation studies that used the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry, and teaches how to build them with the sRtr package (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026). The underlying studies, their cohorts and their regional summaries are specified in the published papers; this plan covers only how a regional summary becomes a map. Reporting follows STROBE and RECORD (Elm et al. 2007; Benchimol et al. 2015) as they apply to a descriptive figure. The reporting map below links each checklist item to a section of this plan.

1. Background and rationale
Each study below reported that use of a donor type or technology varied widely across UNOS regions. A map of the eleven UNOS regions shows that variation at a glance. The original maps were drawn with hand-built region tables, a local Census shapefile and a downloaded list of transplant centers. The sRtr package now holds the region geography and downloads the transplant-center layer, so the same maps can be drawn from a few package calls.

2. Objectives

Primary: for each study, draw a map of the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, with each state shaded by the value of its UNOS region and the eleven region boundaries drawn over the states.
Secondary: overlay the locations of adult heart-transplant centers on the same map.
Teaching: show the original code and the sRtr version side by side for each study.

3. Study design and setting
Descriptive mapping of region-level summaries already computed for each published study. No new cohort is drawn and no new statistic is estimated.

4. Data sources and measurement periods

Regional summaries: one spreadsheet per study in data/regional/, holding one row per UNOS region with the study’s counts and percentages. Each was computed from the UNOS registry for the study period in the table above, as described in its paper.
Region geography: UNOS_regions_sf from sRtr, state polygons from the 2018 Census cartographic boundary file (1:20,000,000) with each state’s UNOS region (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026).
Transplant centers: the HRSA organ procurement and transplantation layer, downloaded with sRtr::get_hrsa_transplant_centers() (Health Resources and Services Administration, n.d.). The original maps used a downloaded copy of an HRSA transplant-center file.


Open: which transplant-center list to map. The HRSA layer describes centers as of the day it is downloaded, not as of each study period. The options are the current layer, a dated snapshot saved once per study, or the original HRSA file (decision D1 in SETUP-NOTES.md; issue to be filed).

5. Study populations and unit definitions

Unit of display: the UNOS region. Every state in a region carries that region’s value.
Geography: the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico are excluded, as in the original maps.
Transplant centers: centers that list heart transplantation, excluding pediatric centers. The original code excluded centers whose name contains “Children”, except Memorial Regional Hospital/Joe DiMaggio Children’s Hospital and Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center & Children’s Hospital, which also transplant adults.


Open: whether to keep the name-based pediatric exclusion with the HRSA layer, whose center names and service lists may differ from the original file (decision D2 in SETUP-NOTES.md; issue to be filed).

6. Estimation
None. Values are taken from each study’s regional summary as published. Proportions stored as fractions are multiplied by 100 for display as percentages.

7. Linkage and geography
Regional summaries join to UNOS_regions_sf by region number. A join that does not match all eleven regions stops the script.

8. Measures and outcomes
As listed for each study in §2.

9. Analysis and interpretation
The maps are descriptive. They show where use of a donor type or technology was higher or lower; they do not estimate why, and a shaded state says nothing about that state alone, only about its region.

10. Missing data and validity requirements
A region with no value is drawn in grey and named in the legend as having no data, not as zero.

11. Sensitivity analyses
None.

12. Disclosure control
Each regional summary holds region-level values that are published in its paper (Madan et al. 2021, 2024, 2025). The spreadsheets and the maps drawn from them are therefore public, as stated by Vagish Hemmige on 2026-11-09 (recorded in SETUP-NOTES.md). No patient-level data are used.

13. Limitations to address in reporting

Shading whole states by region hides variation within a region.
Center locations show where programs are, not how many transplants each performed.
